rv.q: Three-and-a-half hours whip by, crowned by a coup in the epilogue.
The Australian director has made his name wrenching classic dramas into contemporary settings.
This is a masterfully constructed play, turning a familiar story into a consistently tense murder mystery with an artfully splintered timeline.

In the second of the three acts, Montie, unable to forgive Christopher for the death of their daughter Isobel, brutally fells him with poisoned sourdough offered round by her second husband, his clever-fool cousin Jerome (John Macmillan). Which is pretty good going for a couple who spend their days self-medicating on cocaine and champagne.
I had a very good time with The Oresteia until the end when it simply leans too enthusiastically on the idea Augie has lost his mind and degenerates into overwrought silliness.
Powerful performances reveal moments of profound emotion in this lumbering modern-day reimagining of Aeschylus’ tragic trilogy
It’s almost four hours of electrifying spectacle, yet Stone’s all-out vision at times ends up diminishing rather than enhancing his source material.
It is draining, invigorating, frustrating, original and ersatz, with too much thrown at it: Aeschylus, and then some.

In trying to impose a 21st-century aesthetic on one of the cornerstones of Greek tragedy, the writer-director Simon Stone delivers a melodrama (“after Aeschylus and others”) which plays so many games with the source material that it becomes a forced march through terrain that is barely recognisable.
And yet what Simon Stone has created at the Bridge is, without a hint of hyperbole, an absolute marvel of theatre.
The final result is a truly epic and visually stunning achievement, which is sure to be showered with plaudits and gongs come awards season.
There is no doubt Stone’s adaptation is a play for today — and one that the Greeks would be proud of.
The second act of Simon Stone’s The Oresteia is one of the most gripping, visceral and biting hours of drama you are ever likely to see on stage.
The result is a horrifying and compelling tour de force, coming up to three hours of playtime, two of which I spent on the edge of my seat.
This crude Oresteia has none of the dramatic poetry of the original.
By the end of a gruelling three and a half hours, there isn't much moral meat left on the bone, just a slasher gorefest.
This is a reworking without a destination.
What Simon Stone has created here is nothing short of miraculous, bringing a timeless classic to the stage in a way like never before.
It proves that when theatre is this good, it can teach us a real lesson in focus.
Simon Stone’s remarkable reimagining shows us that this will certainly not be the last we see of this electrifying and gripping tragedy.
The result here is uneven and at times self-indulgent, but it also features compelling, inventive theatre.
This is The Oresteia for our times.
This set makes us eavesdroppers on this family’s bloody tragedy whilst also distancing the audience.

cn.t: Stone's audacious modern adaptation of Aeschylus divides critics: some praise its gripping intensity and powerful performances, while others find it overlong and unfocused. The second act earns near-universal acclaim as visceral, unmissable theatre.
